# `nish/net/postgres`

The client side of PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol, version 3.0: a sans-IO connection that writes the frontend's messages into an output buffer and reads the backend's from an input buffer, for a program that owns its socket (`nish:net`) and its loop.

  PG_ARRAY_BAD,
  PG_ARRAY_ELEMENT,
  PG_ARRAY_END,
  PG_ARRAY_NULL,
  PG_BATCH_DONE,
  PG_BATCH_FAILED,
  PG_BATCH_INT,
  PG_BATCH_MISSING,
  PG_BATCH_NONE,

<scalar-callout type="info">

```ts
const config = new PgConfig();
config.user = "app";
config.database = "app";
const nonce = new Array<u8>(18);
crypto.getRandomValues(nonce);
const conn = new PgConnection(config, password, nonce);
// write conn.outputBuffer()[conn.outputStart() .. conn.outputEnd()), then conn.sent(n)
// read into conn.inputBuffer() at conn.inputEnd(), up to conn.inputRoom() bytes, then conn.received(n)
let event: i32 = conn.next();
while (event !== PG_NEED_MORE && event !== PG_FAILED) {
  // PG_READY: authenticated; prepare statements and send queries
  //   conn.prepare("by_id", "select id, name from users where id = $1", [23]); conn.sync()
  //   conn.bindStart("by_id"); conn.paramInt(7); conn.bindEnd(); conn.sync()
  //   or conn.bindStartBinary("by_id") for binary result columns
  // PG_ROW: conn.int(0), conn.colStart(1) .. + conn.colLength(1) in conn.inputBuffer()
  //   after bindStartBinary: conn.binaryInt(0), the text column as before
  // PG_COMPLETE: conn.tagRows(); PG_ERROR: conn.lastError.code
  // PG_GROUP_DONE: one sync()'s group has been answered
  event = conn.next();
}
```

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="Events">

`next()` answers `PG_READY` once, when the server has
authenticated the connection and is ready for queries; `PG_DESCRIBED` when a
prepared statement has been described (`columns` and `columnType(c)` say
what its rows hold, `columns` is 0 when it returns none); `PG_ROW` for each
row, its columns as windows into the input buffer (`colStart(c)`,
`colLength(c)`, -1 for NULL); `PG_COMPLETE` when an execution has finished
(`tagIs("UPDATE")`, `tagRows()`); `PG_ERROR` when a statement in the current
group failed (`lastError`); `PG_NOTICE` for a notice (`lastNotice`);
`PG_GROUP_DONE` when a group has been answered to its end (`groupFailed`,
`txStatus`); and `PG_FAILED`, final: the connection broke a rule or the
server ended it, `failure` says which and `lastError` holds the server's
reason when it gave one. `PG_NEED_MORE` asks for more input.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Windows and buffers">

A column's window, the tag `tagIs` and `tagRows`
read are valid until the next `next()`,
which may move the unread input to the start of the buffer or replace the
buffer with a larger one. Fetch `inputBuffer()` again after every `next()`
rather than keep it; the same holds for `outputBuffer()` after a builder
call.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Groups and pipelining">

Every statement is sent with the extended query
protocol: `prepare` (Parse and Describe), `bindStart`, the `param...` calls
and `bindEnd` (Bind and Execute), `closeStatement` (Close), then `sync()`,
which ends the group. The server answers groups in order and skips the rest
of a group after an error, so one failed statement costs only its own group.
In a failed group, `PG_DESCRIBED` comes once for each `prepare` the server
parsed before the error: a program that counts them knows which statements
exist (named ones last past the group) and which must be prepared again.
Up to `maxInFlight` groups may wait for their answers at once; `canSend()`
says whether another may start, and the builder calls refuse (and write
nothing) when it may not. Nothing waits for a round trip that the protocol
does not need: a program prepares a statement and executes it in the same
flight.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Text results, no copies">

Every parameter is in text format unless it
is one of the binary integer arrays below, and every result column is text
unless the bind asks otherwise. A row is read where it
lies in the input buffer: `next()` frames each message once, validates its
layout, and records each column's start and length in two reused arrays, so
a row costs no allocation. `int`, `bool`, `isNull` and `PgText.timestamp`
decode a column in place; `PgArrayWalker` walks a one-dimensional `text[]`
in place. `columnText(c)` is the one that allocates, a string. An array
parameter is a text array literal too: `paramIntArray` writes an `int8[]`
from an `i64[]` window, and `arrayStart`, `arrayElement`, `arrayInt`,
`arrayNull` and `arrayEnd` build an array one element at a time into the
Bind, so a list needs no string built first. A program whose element was
refused for room can drop the whole bind, unsent, with `bindCancel`.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Binary integer arrays">

`paramInt4Array` and `paramInt8Array` send an
`i64[]` window as an `int4[]` or `int8[]` in PostgreSQL's binary layout:
four or eight bytes an element and no digits to write or parse, which the
benchmark (`bench/postgres/arrays.mjs`) measured at about a tenth of the
text encoder's client CPU, and at 1,000 elements a 51% cut in the server's
on `unnest` for `int8[]`, 30% for `int4[]`.
`binaryArrayStart(oid)`, `binaryArrayInt` and `binaryArrayNull` build one
element at a time, NULLs included, and `arrayEnd` closes it. The Bind's
format codes stay a single zero word while every parameter is text; the
first binary one makes `bindEnd` write a code for each, so an all-text bind
costs nothing more. An `int4` element outside `int4` panics rather than
wrapping. The element type must match the statement's parameter: the server
answers a mismatch with `ErrorResponse` (42804) for that execution, and the
connection goes on.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Binary results">

A bind opened with `bindStartBinary` instead of
`bindStart` asks for every result column in binary format: an `int8` is
eight bytes, a `timestamptz` eight bytes of microseconds since 2000, a
`bool` one byte, so there is nothing to parse and less on the wire.
`binaryInt`, `binaryBool` and `binaryFloat` read them in place, and
`PgBinary`'s `timestamp` and `iso` write a time as `PgText.timestamp` does.
A `text` column is the same bytes in either format, so `columnText` and the
column windows read it unchanged. The program knows which of its binds
asked for which, and reads each execution's rows with the matching
decoders. A `PgBatcher` with `binary` set opens each batch this way and
reads its routing ordinal with `binaryInt`, so its rows are binary too.
`PgBinaryArray` walks a one-dimensional `int2[]`, `int4[]` or `int8[]`
column in its binary layout, and refuses any other array (a `text[]` or a
multi-dimensional one among them).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Authentication">

SCRAM-SHA-256 (RFC 5802, RFC 7677) or none (`trust`).
The password arrives as a `Secret<u8[]>`; the connection keeps a copy in a
holder that is wiped as soon as the proof is computed, or when the
connection fails or is disposed. The server's signature is checked in
constant time before `AuthenticationOk` is believed, and an
`AuthenticationOk` that skips the end of an exchange SCRAM began is refused.
Cleartext and MD5 passwords, and SASL mechanisms other than SCRAM-SHA-256,
are refused: with no TLS here the first sends the password as it is, and the
second is a hash any eavesdropper can replay. The password's bytes are used
as they are, without SASLprep (RFC 4013): an ASCII password works, and a
non-ASCII one works only when it is already in the form SASLprep would give
(PostgreSQL itself falls back to the raw bytes when it cannot prepare one).
`docs/security/postgres.md` is the record.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-callout type="warning">

**Caps.** `PgConfig` bounds what a server can make the client hold: the
longest message (`maxMessage`), the widest row (`maxColumns`) and the SCRAM
iteration count (`minIterations`, `maxIterations`); and what a program can
queue unsent (`maxOutput`), past which a builder call answers false. A
message longer than the cap, a length below 4, a layout that does not add
up, a message the protocol does not allow at that point (COPY among them),
an encoding other than UTF-8, and a `DateStyle` other than ISO or a
`TimeZone` other than UTC (at startup or after a `SET`), each fail the
connection with their own `failure` code. The constructor panics on a cap
out of range, as on a missing user or a short nonce.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="Pools">

`PgPool` holds up to `size` connections to one server and a FIFO
queue of up to `queueSize` requests, still sans-IO: `wanted()` names a slot
that needs a socket, `connect(slot, nonce)` starts its connection, and the
program moves its bytes as above through `connection(slot)`. A request is a
ticket from `request()`; `dispatch()` gives the oldest to the ready
connection with the fewest groups in flight (or, with `PgConfig.pack`, to the
first ready one with room, so a burst fills few connections in fuller
writes), the program builds its group and ends it with `send()`, and `next(slot)` reads that connection's events with
`ticket` naming the request. Statements given to `register` are prepared on
each connection ahead of its first request. A connection that fails reports
`PG_LOST` for each request it took, then `PG_FAILED`; the program closes the
socket and the slot is built again on its next use.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Carrier">

`PgCarrier`, in `nish/net/postgres-carrier`, moves a pool's
bytes on an `HttpHandler`'s loop, so a route handler queries without
blocking its worker. It is a module of its own because it reads sockets,
the clock and the entropy source, and this one reaches none of them.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Batching">

`PgBatcher` turns many reads of one row shape by key — a user
by id, an article by slug — into one execution of a statement over
`unnest($1) with ordinality`. `addInt` or `addText` queues a request's key
and tag; `take(conn)` binds the oldest waiting, each distinct key once (past
`PG_BATCH_PROBES` slots of its table probe, a key is bound again), up
to `maxRequests` and `maxBytes`, and answers a run's handle; `row`, `end`
and `fail` take that execution's events (a handle already answered makes
them a no-op counted in `stray`, so a server's late event cannot panic),
routing each row by its ordinal (checked first: a server's ordinal is
refused before it routes anything), and `next(run)` answers
`PG_BATCH_ROW`, then `PG_BATCH_DONE`, `PG_BATCH_MISSING` or
`PG_BATCH_FAILED`, for each request. The statement orders its rows by
ordinal, so a key's last events come as soon as a later key's row does;
with `sorted` false it does not (no Sort node, when `orderBy` is ""), rows
are answered in whatever order they come, and every last event waits for
the execution's end. It reads no clock, and the batcher
itself allocates only in its constructor (the connection's output buffer a
take writes into may still grow, up to its `maxOutput`); when to take is
the program's.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Batch timing">

`PgBatchClock` is one answer to when: given the time in
microseconds, `check(now, inFlight)` says a batch is due once
max(`minCount`, the moving average of recent batch sizes × `factor`) items
wait, once the oldest has waited `maxWaitUs`, or, with the idle bypass on,
at once when nothing is in flight and fewer than `lightCount` arrived in the
last `lightWindowUs`; `average`, `lastSize`, `lastReason` and `startsFor`
are its metrics. Its defaults are the fixed window. `PgBatcher.takeDue`
takes only when its clock says so, and `PgBatchTurns` lets one free
connection collect while the others execute, woken only when its batch is
due. Neither reads a clock or allocates per item.

</scalar-detail>

Written from PostgreSQL's "Frontend/Backend Protocol" chapter (version 18)
and RFC 5802 and RFC 7677; not ported from another implementation.

## pgTarget

The target `host` and `port` name, as libpq's `host` and `port` do: a host
starting with `/` or `@` is the socket `<host>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`, any other
a TCP host. The host is not percent-decoded. A port outside 1 to 65535, an
empty host, a `,` (more than one host) or a NUL byte is refused, and so is
a socket path over 107 bytes (an `@` name over 107 after its `@`), never
cut short.

```ts
function pgTarget(
  host: string,
  port: i32,
): PgTarget
```

<scalar-field name="host" type="string" required>
</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="port" type="i32" required>

## pgTargetUrl

The target a `postgres://` or `postgresql://` URL names, as libpq reads
one: `postgres://[user[:password]@][host][:port][/dbname][?key=value&...]`.
The host, the port and every query key and value are percent-decoded, so a
socket directory is written `%2Ftmp` or passed as `?host=/tmp`; a `host` or
`port` in the query overrides the authority's, and other keys are ignored.
The user, password and database are not read here, but a bad escape in them
still refuses the URL. A `%` without two hex digits after it, `%00`, or a
part that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8 is `PG_TARGET_BAD_ESCAPE`.
The user information ends at the first `@`, as in libpq; a raw `@` after a
`?` or after that first `@` in the authority, or a raw NUL byte anywhere,
is `PG_TARGET_BAD_HOST`, as is a URL with no host anywhere, where libpq
would use its default socket directory. An empty port or query value is
refused, where libpq would take it as unset.
The decoded host is then resolved as `pgTarget` resolves one.

```ts
function pgTargetUrl(url: string): PgTarget
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="url" type="string" required>
</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="PgTarget">
</scalar-field>

## PgArrayWalker

A walk over a one-dimensional `text[]` column in place: `start` the
column, then `next()` until `PG_ARRAY_END` or `PG_ARRAY_BAD`. Each element
is the window `[start, start + length)` of the column's buffer; a quoted
element with a backslash escape in it has `escaped` set, and `copy` writes
its bytes unescaped. An unquoted `NULL`, in any case, is `PG_ARRAY_NULL`.
Dimension decorations (`[1:2]={...}`) and nested arrays are `PG_ARRAY_BAD`.

```ts
class PgArrayWalker
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgArrayWalker()` |  |
| `escaped: boolean` | Whether the current element holds a backslash escape. |
| `length: i32` | The current element's length, escapes included. |
| `start: i32` | The current element's first byte in the buffer. |
| `begin(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): void` | Starts a walk over `b[start, start + length)`. |
| `copy(out: u8[], at: i32): i32` | Writes the current element, unescaped, to `out[at, ...)`; answers its length, or -1 when it does not fit. |
| `next(): i32` | The next element: `PG_ARRAY_ELEMENT`, `PG_ARRAY_NULL`, `PG_ARRAY_END` or `PG_ARRAY_BAD`. |

## PgBatchClock

Says when to start a batch, sans-IO like `PgBatcher`: the program passes
the time, in microseconds from any fixed point, and the clock reads none.
It keeps the arrival time of each waiting item, oldest first, and the
moving average (EWMA) of the batches started. `check` answers the reason a
batch should start now, or `PG_CLOCK_WAIT`: the target count is waiting
(the larger of `minCount` and the average times `factor`, never more than
`maxCount`), the oldest has waited `maxWaitUs`, or, with the idle bypass on,
nothing is in flight and the load is light. `deadline()` is when the timer
fires, for a poll's timeout.

Under a backlog the target is already waiting, so the batch starts by count
the moment a connection is free, and nothing waits on the timer; a batch
started by count is at least the target, so the average does not fall
while the backlog lasts. Only a batch the timer or the bypass starts can
be smaller than the average and pull it down, as the load falls.

The program mirrors its queue: `arrived(now)` for each item queued,
`started(size, now)` for each batch taken, oldest items first. A
`PgBatcher` does both itself through `takeDue`; a program forming its own
batches calls them by hand. The fields after a start are for metrics.
Everything is allocated in the constructor; nothing per item.

```ts
class PgBatchClock
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBatchClock(config: PgBatchClockConfig)` | A clock for `config`; panics when a setting is out of the range its field names. |
| `average: f64` | The moving average of the batch sizes started, 0 before the first. |
| `lastReason: i32` | Why the last batch started: the reason `check` last answered, `PG_CLOCK_WAIT` when it started without one. |
| `lastSize: i32` | The size of the last batch started, 0 before the first. |
| `lastWaitUs: i64` | How long the oldest item of the last batch waited, in microseconds. |
| `readonly maxCount: i32` |  |
| `arrived(nowUs: i64): boolean` | Records an item queued at `nowUs`; false when `queueSize` are waiting. A time before the last one given counts as the last one, so a clock that steps back cannot make an item older than its neighbours. |
| `check(nowUs: i64, inFlight: i32): i32` | The reason a batch should start at `nowUs`, with `inFlight` batches (or groups) still running, or `PG_CLOCK_WAIT`. It only says; the program starts the batch when a connection is free, then calls `started`. |
| `deadline(): i64` | When the oldest waiting item has waited `maxWaitUs`, in the caller's microseconds; -1 when none waits. |
| `started(size: i32, nowUs: i64): void` | Records a batch of the `size` oldest items started at `nowUs`, and moves the average toward it; the first batch sets it. Panics when `size` is below 1 or more than are waiting or than `maxCount`. |
| `startsFor(reason: i32): i64` | How many batches have started for `reason`, one of the `PG_CLOCK_*` (`PG_CLOCK_WAIT` counts those started without a due `check`). |
| `target(): i32` | The count that starts a batch now: the larger of `minCount` and the average times `factor`, at most `maxCount`. |
| `waiting(): i32` | The number of items waiting. |

## PgBatchClockConfig

When a `PgBatchClock` starts a batch. The defaults are the fixed window:
a batch starts when `maxCount` items wait or the oldest has waited
`maxWaitUs`, whatever the load. To adapt, set `factor` (1.1 is a good
start), lower `minCount` (16), and turn on the idle bypass (`lightCount`
8); `bench/pg-batch-clock.ts` measures each against the fixed windows.

```ts
class PgBatchClockConfig
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBatchClockConfig()` |  |
| `factor: f64` | The share of the recent batch size that must wait before a batch starts, 0 to 64; 0 leaves the average out, the fixed window. Above 1 batches grow until the timer bounds them (fewer statements, more wait); below 1 they shrink toward `minCount`. |
| `lightCount: i32` | The idle bypass: with nothing in flight and fewer than `lightCount` items arrived in the last `lightWindowUs`, an item goes at once. 0, the default, turns it off; up to 1024. |
| `lightWindowUs: i64` | The window `lightCount` counts arrivals over, in microseconds, 0 to a minute. |
| `maxCount: i32` | The most items one batch takes, `PgBatchConfig.maxRequests` for a batcher's clock. The count to start never passes it, so a backlog always starts by count. |
| `maxWaitUs: i64` | The longest the oldest item waits for others, in microseconds, 0 to a minute: the most latency batching adds when the load is light. |
| `minCount: i32` | The fewest items that start a batch by count. Lower answers sooner under light load and spends more statements per item; `maxCount` is the fixed window. |
| `queueSize: i32` | The most items waiting, 1 to 2^20: `PgBatchConfig.queueSize` for a batcher's clock. |
| `weight: f64` | How far each batch moves the average, over 0 up to 1. Higher follows a change of load sooner and jumps more on one odd batch. |

## PgBatchConfig

What a `PgBatcher` sends: one statement shape, its key, and its caps.

```ts
class PgBatchConfig
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBatchConfig()` |  |
| `binary: boolean` | Whether every row of a batch comes in binary format, read with the binary decoders and its ordinal by `binaryInt`; false for text. |
| `keyType: i32` | `PG_BATCH_INT` or `PG_BATCH_TEXT`. |
| `maxBytes: i32` | The most bytes the key array parameter takes, `{}` included. |
| `maxRequests: i32` | The most requests one execution answers. |
| `name: string` | The prepared statement's name, which `PgBatcher.sql` is prepared under. |
| `orderBy: string` | Columns of `t`, the query's rows, ordering the rows of one key: `t.created_at desc`; "" for none. |
| `queueBytes: i32` | The most bytes of text keys waiting. |
| `queueSize: i32` | The most requests waiting. |
| `runs: i32` | The most executions in flight at once. |
| `select: string` | The query for one key, `q.key`: `select id, title from articles where slug = q.key`. |
| `sorted: boolean` | Whether the statement orders its rows by ordinal, so each key's last event comes as soon as a later key's row does. False drops `q.ord` from the `order by` (and the Sort node it costs, when `orderBy` is ""): rows route in whatever order they come, and every request's last event waits for the execution's end. |

## PgBatchTurns

Turn-taking for a program with several connections that forms batches
with one `PgBatchClock`: one free connection, the collector, gathers while
the others execute, and a push wakes it only when its batch is due, not on
every item. Sans-IO like the clock: a slot is the program's own number for
a connection, 0 to `size - 1`, and the answer to each call is the slot to
wake, or `PG_TURNS_NONE`.

The collector is the lowest-numbered free slot. `push(now)` records an item
and answers the collector when this item makes the batch due; `poll(now)`
answers it when the timer has made it due, at `deadline()`. Once a slot is
named, no other is until it calls `started(slot, size, now)` with the batch
it took, or `release(slot)` when it took none. `finished(slot, now)` frees
a slot after its batch. Both `started` and `finished` answer the next slot
to wake when a batch is already due, as under a backlog: nothing waits on
the timer then. The in-flight count the idle bypass reads is the slots
holding a batch.

```ts
class PgBatchTurns
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBatchTurns(clock: PgBatchClock, size: i32)` | Turns over `size` slots (1 to 1024), all free; panics on a size out of range. |
| `readonly clock: PgBatchClock` | The clock the turns read and record into. |
| `readonly size: i32` | The number of slots. |
| `collector(): i32` | The slot that collects: the lowest-numbered free one, or `PG_TURNS_NONE` when every slot holds a batch. |
| `deadline(): i64` | When the collector's timer fires, `PgBatchClock.deadline()`; -1 when nothing waits. |
| `finished(slot: i32, nowUs: i64): i32` | Records `slot`'s batch done at `nowUs`, and answers the slot to wake. Panics on a slot out of range or holding no batch. |
| `inFlight(): i32` | The number of slots holding a batch. |
| `poll(nowUs: i64): i32` | The slot to wake at `nowUs`, when a batch is due and no slot is named already. |
| `push(nowUs: i64): i32` | Records an item queued at `nowUs` and answers the slot to wake, or `PG_TURNS_FULL` when the clock is full. |
| `release(slot: i32): void` | Gives back a wake that started nothing, so the next push or poll can wake a slot again. |
| `started(slot: i32, size: i32, nowUs: i64): i32` | Records `slot` starting a batch of `size` items at `nowUs`, and answers the next slot to wake. Panics on a slot out of range or holding a batch already, or as `PgBatchClock.started`. |

## PgBatcher

Batches keyed reads of one statement shape, sans-IO like `PgConnection`:
it reads no clock and makes no socket. Each request is a key and the
caller's `tag`, queued by `addInt` or `addText`. When a connection is free,
`take(conn)` binds up to `maxRequests` of them, and up to `maxBytes` of
keys, as one execution of `sql`, each distinct key once (a key whose
probe of the batcher's table passes 1024 slots, which takes keys chosen to
collide, is bound again and answered the same), and answers the
execution's run handle. Each `PG_ROW` of that execution goes to
`row(run, conn)`, its `PG_COMPLETE` to `end(run)`, and an error or a lost
connection to `fail(run)`; after each, `next(run)` answers events until
`PG_BATCH_NONE`, `tag` naming the request each is about. Every row goes to
every request for its key, and every request gets one last event:
`PG_BATCH_DONE`, `PG_BATCH_MISSING` or `PG_BATCH_FAILED`. Sorted (the
default), rows come in key order and a key's last events come as soon as
a later key's row does; with `sorted` false, rows come in any order, each
answered at once, and every last event waits for `end` or `fail`, then
comes in key order. A batch with
`binary` set comes in binary format: its rows are read with the binary
decoders, `binaryInt` for each ordinal, and the caller's `binary.failed`
is left as it was.

Nothing outlives its execution: a run is free again once the events
`end` or `fail` owe are answered, and its handle is then spent. What the
server or the network can send after that — a second `PG_COMPLETE`, a row
or an error after one, a lost connection — goes to a spent handle, and
`row`, `end` and `fail` count it in `stray` and do nothing, even once
`take` has given the run out again under a new handle. The ordinal each
row carries comes from the server and is checked before it routes
anything. What panics is only the program's own misuse: a handle out of
the range `take` can give (-1 or any negative, or `runs` * 2^20 or more),
or `row`, `end` or `fail` before `next(run)` has answered `PG_BATCH_NONE`
for the event before. A handle in that range that `take` never gave is
spent like any other: counted in `stray`, not a panic.

```ts
class PgBatcher
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBatcher(config: PgBatchConfig)` | A batcher for `config`; panics when a name or query is empty or holds a NUL, or a cap is out of range. |
| `readonly maxRequests: i32` | The most requests one execution takes, from `PgBatchConfig.maxRequests`. |
| `readonly name: string` | The prepared statement's name. |
| `refused: i32` | The number of runs failed by a bad ordinal (missing, NULL, not an integer, or naming no key still open; with `sorted` false, any key of the run is open), stopping at 2^31 - 1: each counts its first refused row, and the rows after it, dropped with the failed run, are not counted. |
| `readonly sql: string` | The statement to prepare under `name` (`PgPool.register` or `PgConnection.prepare`, no parameter types); each row's last column is the ordinal it routes by. |
| `stray: i32` | The number of `row`, `end` and `fail` calls on a spent handle, each ignored, stopping at 2^31 - 1. |
| `tag: i32` | The request the last `next(run)` answered about; -1 for none. |
| `addInt(key: i64, tag: i32): boolean` | Queues a request for the int8 `key`; false when `queueSize` are waiting. Panics on a text batcher. |
| `addText(bytes: u8[], start: i32, length: i32, tag: i32): boolean` | Queues a request for the text key `bytes[start, start + length)`, which is copied; false when the key is not UTF-8 or holds a NUL (the server would fail the whole execution over it), `queueSize` are waiting, the key would not fit in `queueBytes` beside those waiting, or it is too long for one execution's `maxBytes`. Panics on an int8 batcher, or when the window is not inside `bytes`. |
| `end(r: i32): void` | Ends run `r`'s execution, on its `PG_COMPLETE`: `next(r)` then closes every request left. Ignores a spent handle, and panics, as `row` does. |
| `fail(r: i32): void` | Fails run `r`'s execution, on its `PG_ERROR` or `PG_LOST`: `next(r)` then answers `PG_BATCH_FAILED` for every request left. Ignores a spent handle, and panics, as `row` does. |
| `next(r: i32): i32` | The next event `row`, `end` or `fail` owes on run `r`, with `tag` the request it is about; `PG_BATCH_NONE`, and `tag` -1, when there is none. Once `end` or `fail` has had all its events the run is over, free for `take` again, and its handle spent: `PG_BATCH_NONE` ever after. Panics on a handle `take` cannot give. |
| `row(r: i32, conn: PgConnection): boolean` | Routes `conn`'s current row, of run `r`'s execution, by the ordinal in its last column: `next(r)` then answers `PG_BATCH_ROW` for each request of its key, after the last events of the keys before it (with `sorted` false, at once: no last event comes before `end`). False, and the row dropped, when the run has failed; and when the ordinal is NULL, not an integer, or names no key still open (one out of range, or, sorted, one before the key the last row was for): that counts in `refused` and fails the run; and on a spent handle, which counts in `stray`. Panics on a handle `take` cannot give, or when the run's events are not all answered. |
| `shed(): i32` | Drops the oldest waiting request and answers its tag, or -1 when none waits: for a program that cannot reach the server to fail requests rather than hold them. |
| `take(conn: PgConnection): i32` | Binds the oldest waiting requests on `conn` as one execution of `sql`, prepared there already, and answers its run's handle, which names this execution and no later one of the same run; the caller ends the group (`sync()`, or `PgPool.send()`). It takes up to `maxRequests` requests, oldest first, and stops at the first whose key would pass `maxBytes` or the connection's `maxOutput`; those not taken stay queued. -1, and nothing written, when none waits, every run is in flight, or `conn` refused the bind or the first key. |
| `takeDue(conn: PgConnection, clock: PgBatchClock, nowUs: i64, inFlight: i32): i32` | `take(conn)` when `clock` says a batch is due at `nowUs`, with `inFlight` of the program's executions or groups running (`PgPool.inFlight()`), and the batch taken recorded in `clock`; -1 when it is not due or `take` answers -1. The program calls `clock.arrived(now)` for each request it adds. Panics when the clock's waiting count is not this batcher's, or its `maxCount` is below `maxRequests`. |
| `waiting(): i32` | The number of requests waiting for `take`. |

## PgBinary

Decoders for PostgreSQL's binary format, in place, for the rows of a bind
that `bindStartBinary` opened; a bad input sets `failed`, which stays set.
A `text` or `varchar` column's bytes are the same in either format, so
`columnText`, `colStart` and `colLength` read it as they read a text one.

```ts
class PgBinary
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBinary()` |  |
| `failed: boolean` | Whether a decode since the last `reset()` was given something it could not read. |
| `bool(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): boolean` | A `bool` column: one byte, 1 or 0; false and `failed` otherwise. |
| `float(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): f64` | A `float8` column: eight bytes, IEEE 754 big-endian; 0 and `failed` otherwise. |
| `int(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): i64` | An `int2`, `int4` or `int8` column, told apart by its length (2, 4 or 8 bytes, big-endian two's complement); 0 and `failed` for any other length, NULL's -1 among them. A `timestamptz` or `timestamp` reads as an `int8`: microseconds since 2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, which `iso` writes out. |
| `iso(micros: i64, out: u8[], at: i32): i32` | `micros`, microseconds since 2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, written to `out[at, at + 24)` as `2024-01-02T03:04:05.123Z`: the microseconds cut, not rounded, to milliseconds, as `PgText.timestamp` cuts the same time. Answers 24, or -1 and `failed` with `out` untouched for a year outside 0001–9999 (`infinity` and `-infinity` among them) or no room in `out`. |
| `reset(): void` | Clears `failed`. |
| `timestamp(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32, out: u8[], at: i32): i32` | A `timestamptz` or `timestamp` column, written to `out[at, at + 24)` as `iso` writes it. Answers 24, or -1 and `failed` for a column that is not eight bytes or a time `iso` refuses. |

## PgBinaryArray

A walk over a one-dimensional `int2[]`, `int4[]` or `int8[]` column in
PostgreSQL's binary array layout, in place: `begin` the column, then
`next()` until `PG_ARRAY_END` or `PG_ARRAY_BAD`, and `int()` decodes the
current element through `binary`. The header is `ndim`, `hasnull` and the
element OID, then for `ndim` 1 the dimension's length and lower bound (the
bound is read and not used); each element is a length word and its bytes,
and a NULL is a length of -1 with no bytes. `ndim` 0 is the empty array.
Every refusal sets `binary.failed`: an `ndim` above 1, another element
type, an element whose length is not its type's size, a NULL when
`hasnull` is 0, a column cut short, or bytes after the last element. The
walk allocates nothing, and it reads nothing outside the column.

```ts
class PgBinaryArray
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgBinaryArray(binary: PgBinary)` |  |
| `count: i32` | The number of elements the header gives: 0 for an empty array. |
| `elementOid: i32` | The element type's OID, 20, 21 or 23, once `begin` has read a header it accepts. |
| `length: i32` | The current element's length: its type's size, or 0 for a NULL. |
| `start: i32` | The current element's first byte in the buffer. |
| `begin(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): void` | Starts a walk over `b[start, start + length)`; a header this walker does not read is refused. |
| `int(): i64` | The current element as an integer, through `PgBinary.int`; a NULL, or a walk that was refused, sets `binary.failed`. |
| `next(): i32` | The next element: `PG_ARRAY_ELEMENT`, `PG_ARRAY_NULL`, `PG_ARRAY_END` or `PG_ARRAY_BAD`. |

## PgConfig

The caps a connection enforces, and the startup parameters it sends.

```ts
class PgConfig
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgConfig()` |  |
| `applicationName: string` | `application_name`, shown in `pg_stat_activity`; empty sends none. |
| `database: string` | The database; empty means the server's default, the role's name. |
| `inputSize: i32` | The input buffer's first size, in bytes; it grows to a message's length, up to `maxMessage` + 1. |
| `maxColumns: i32` | The widest row; past it, `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG`. PostgreSQL's own limit is 1664. |
| `maxInFlight: i32` | The most groups waiting for their answers at once. |
| `maxIterations: i32` | The most SCRAM iterations computed, so a server cannot make the client spin. |
| `maxMessage: i32` | The longest backend message, in bytes, its type byte aside; past it, `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG`. |
| `maxOutput: i32` | The most bytes the builder calls may queue unsent; a call that would pass it answers false and writes nothing, so a program that never drains its output cannot grow the buffer without bound. |
| `minIterations: i32` | The fewest SCRAM iterations accepted; 4096 is PostgreSQL's default and RFC 7677's floor. |
| `options: string` | The startup `options` parameter (`-c name=value ...`); empty sends none. |
| `pack: boolean` | Read by `PgPool` only: whether `dispatch()` packs requests onto the first ready connection with room, filling it to `maxInFlight` before the next, rather than spreading them over every connection, fewest in flight first. Fewer connections in use send fuller writes, fewer packets, which pays on a lossy link to the server; a connection is still wanted only once every ready one is full. |
| `user: string` | The role to connect as; required. |

## PgConnection

One connection to a PostgreSQL server, sans IO: the program moves bytes
between the socket and the two buffers, and `next()` says what they meant.

```ts
class PgConnection
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgConnection(config: PgConfig, password: Secret<u8[]>, nonce: u8[])` | A connection that has queued its startup message. `password` is copied, so the caller may wipe its own; `nonce` must be at least 18 bytes from a cryptographic random source (`crypto.getRandomValues`), and is fixed only in a test. |
| `backendPid: i32` | The server's process id, from BackendKeyData. |
| `readonly binary: PgBinary` | The decoders `binaryInt`, `binaryBool` and `binaryFloat` use, for a bind `bindStartBinary` opened; `binary.failed` as `text.failed`. |
| `columns: i32` | The columns of the current row, or of the statement just described. |
| `failure: i32` | Why the connection failed, `PG_ERR_NONE` while it has not. |
| `groupFailed: boolean` | Whether a statement in the group `PG_GROUP_DONE` just finished failed. |
| `inFlight: i32` | The number of groups sent and not yet answered. |
| `lastError: PgError \| null` | The last ErrorResponse, kept until the next. |
| `lastNotice: PgError \| null` | The last NoticeResponse, kept until the next. |
| `notices: i32` | The number of notices received, stopping at 2^31 - 1. |
| `serverVersion: string` | The server's `server_version` parameter. |
| `readonly text: PgText` | The decoders `int`, `bool` and `isNull` use; `text.failed` says whether one was given a column it could not read. |
| `txStatus: i32` | The transaction status the last `PG_GROUP_DONE` reported: `I` idle, `T` in a transaction, `E` in a failed one (as a byte). |
| `arrayElement(bytes: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): boolean` | A text element from `bytes[start, start + length)`, UTF-8, quoted with `"` and `\` escaped; false, and nothing written, when there is no room. Panics when no array is open or the window is not inside `bytes`. |
| `arrayEnd(): void` | Ends the open array parameter, text or binary; never refused for room, which its elements kept. Panics when no array is open. |
| `arrayInt(value: i64): boolean` | An integer element, in decimal; false, and nothing written, when there is no room. Panics when no array is open. |
| `arrayNull(): boolean` | A NULL element; false, and nothing written, when there is no room. Panics when no array is open. |
| `arrayStart(): boolean` | Opens an array parameter, `{}` so far; false as the `param...` calls are. |
| `binaryArrayInt(value: i64): boolean` | An integer element of the open binary array; false, and nothing written, when there is no room. Panics when no binary array is open, or when it is an `int4[]` and `value` is outside `int4`. |
| `binaryArrayNull(): boolean` | A NULL element of the open binary array, length -1; false, and nothing written, when there is no room. Panics when no binary array is open. |
| `binaryArrayStart(elementOid: i32): boolean` | Opens a binary array parameter of `elementOid`'s elements; false as the `param...` calls are. Panics on another OID, or while an array is open. |
| `binaryBool(c: i32): boolean` | Binary column `c` as a boolean; NULL or a bad value sets `binary.failed`. |
| `binaryFloat(c: i32): f64` | Binary column `c`, a `float8`, as an f64; NULL or another length sets `binary.failed`. |
| `binaryInt(c: i32): i64` | Binary column `c`, an `int2`, `int4`, `int8` or a time's microseconds, as an integer; NULL or another length sets `binary.failed`. |
| `bindCancel(): boolean` | Drops the open bind, and the array open in it, unsent, so that a program whose parameter was refused for room can send the group without it; a group the bind opened is closed again. False when no bind is open. |
| `bindEnd(): boolean` | Ends the Bind (every result column in text, or in binary after `bindStartBinary`) and queues its Execute, for every row. False, and nothing written, when no bind is open; never for room, which the calls before it kept. |
| `bindStart(name: string): boolean` | Starts a Bind of the prepared statement `name`; its parameters follow, in order, then `bindEnd()`. False as `prepare` is. |
| `bindStartBinary(name: string): boolean` | `bindStart`, asking for every result column of the execution in binary format rather than text: fixed-size integers, booleans, floats and times, read in place by `binaryInt`, `binaryBool`, `binaryFloat` and `binary.timestamp`. A `text` column's bytes are the same in either format, so `columnText` and the column windows read it as before. An `int2[]`, `int4[]` or `int8[]` column comes in PostgreSQL's binary layout, which `PgBinaryArray` reads; a `text[]` or `numeric` column comes in that layout too, and no decoder here reads it. `PgBatcher` opens its batches with this when its `binary` is set, and reads their routing ordinals with `binaryInt`. Its `bindEnd()` writes two bytes more, kept free under `maxOutput` from here on. False as `prepare` is. |
| `bool(c: i32): boolean` | Column `c` as a boolean; NULL or a bad value sets `text.failed`. |
| `canSend(): boolean` | Whether another group may start, or the open one take another message. |
| `closed(): i32` | Reports the end of the stream: unless it already has, the connection fails with `PG_ERR_CLOSED`. |
| `closeStatement(name: string): boolean` | Close: forgets the prepared statement `name`. False as `prepare` is. |
| `colLength(c: i32): i32` | Column `c`'s length, -1 for NULL. |
| `colStart(c: i32): i32` | Column `c`'s first byte in `inputBuffer()`. |
| `columnText(c: i32): string` | Column `c` as a string; the one result read that allocates. "" for NULL. |
| `columnType(c: i32): i32` | Column `c` of the statement just described: its type's OID (23 is `int4`, 25 `text`). |
| `dispose(): void` | Wipes the password if the connection still holds it. A program that drops a connection before it is ready calls this. |
| `inputBuffer(): u8[]` | The input buffer: read from the socket into it at `inputEnd()`. |
| `inputEnd(): i32` | Where the next byte read goes. |
| `inputRoom(): i32` | How many bytes may be read into the input buffer now. |
| `int(c: i32): i64` | Column `c` as an integer; NULL or a bad value sets `text.failed`. |
| `isNull(c: i32): boolean` | Whether column `c` is NULL. |
| `next(): i32` | The next event from the input. |
| `outputBuffer(): u8[]` | The output buffer: write `[outputStart(), outputEnd())` to the socket. |
| `outputEnd(): i32` | One past the last byte that may be sent: a Bind still open is held back until `bindEnd()` has written its lengths. |
| `outputStart(): i32` | The first byte not yet sent. |
| `paramBytes(bytes: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): boolean` | A text parameter from `bytes[start, start + length)`, UTF-8; false too when the window is not inside `bytes`. |
| `paramInt(value: i64): boolean` | An integer parameter, in decimal. |
| `paramInt4Array(values: i64[], start: i32, count: i32): boolean` | An `int4[]` parameter in binary from `values[start, start + count)`; false as the `param...` calls are. Panics, writing nothing, when the window is not inside `values` or an element is outside `int4`. |
| `paramInt8Array(values: i64[], start: i32, count: i32): boolean` | An `int8[]` parameter in binary from `values[start, start + count)`; false as the `param...` calls are. Panics when the window is not inside `values`. |
| `paramIntArray(values: i64[], start: i32, count: i32): boolean` | An `int8[]` parameter from `values[start, start + count)`, in decimal; panics when the range is not inside `values`. |
| `paramNull(): boolean` | A NULL parameter. |
| `paramText(value: string): boolean` | A text parameter. |
| `paramTextArray(items: string[]): boolean` | A `text[]` parameter: every element quoted, `"` and `` escaped. |
| `passwordWiped(): boolean` | Whether every byte of the connection's copy of the password is zero: true once the proof is computed, the connection has failed or `dispose()` has run (and for an empty password). It reads the copy itself, so a test can see the wipe happen; a program has no use for it. |
| `prepare(name: string, sql: string, paramTypes: i32[]): boolean` | Parse and Describe: prepares `sql` as the statement `name` ("" is the unnamed one), its parameters' types given by `paramTypes` (OIDs, 0 to let the server infer one, and parameters past the array are inferred too). The server answers `PG_DESCRIBED`. False, and nothing written, when `canSend()` is false, a bind is open, `name` or `sql` holds a NUL, or the message would pass `maxOutput`. |
| `receive(src: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): i32` | Copies what fits of `src[start, start + length)` into the input buffer; answers how much. |
| `received(n: i32): void` | Records that `n` bytes were read into the input buffer at `inputEnd()`. |
| `sent(n: i32): void` | Records that `n` bytes from `outputStart()` were written to the socket. |
| `sync(): boolean` | Sync: ends the open group, which the server answers with `PG_GROUP_DONE`. False when no group is open or a bind is; never for room. |
| `tagIs(word: string): boolean` | Whether the tag of the execution just completed starts with the word `word` (`INSERT`, `SELECT`, ...). |
| `tagRows(): i64` | The row count the tag ends with (`INSERT 0 3` is 3, `SELECT 5` is 5), or -1 when it has none or it does not fit an i64. |
| `terminate(): void` | Terminate: tells the server the connection is ending; close the socket once it is sent. A bind still open is dropped unsent. |

## PgPool

A pool of connections to one server, sans-IO like `PgConnection`: it makes
no socket and reads no clock, and says which slot needs a socket and when.
Its size is a cap, and no connection is made until a request needs one and
no ready connection has room.

A request is a ticket from `request()`, queued in FIFO order. `dispatch()`
hands the queue's head to the ready connection with the fewest groups in
flight, or under `PgConfig.pack` the lowest-numbered ready one with room,
never past `maxInFlight` on one; the program builds the request's
group on `connection(slot)` and ends it with `send()`, not `sync()`.
`next(slot)` then reads that connection's events, `ticket` naming the
request each is about. A connection that fails reports `PG_LOST` for each
request it took with it, then `PG_FAILED`, and is built again on its next
use. Statements given to `register` are prepared on each connection in the
same group as its first request, so a request may bind them at once.

```ts
class PgPool
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgPool(config: PgConfig, password: Secret<u8[]>, size: i32, queueSize: i32)` | A pool of up to `size` connections (1 to 1024) and up to `queueSize` waiting requests (1 to 2^20). `password` is copied and kept until `dispose()`, since a connection is made again after a failure. Panics as `PgConnection` does on `config`, and on a `maxInFlight` over 1024. |
| `readonly size: i32` | The number of slots, the most connections the pool makes. |
| `ticket: i32` | The request the last `dispatch()`, or event from `next(slot)`, is about; -1 for none. |
| `connect(slot: i32, nonce: u8[]): void` | Makes the wanted `slot`'s connection, `nonce` as `PgConnection` takes it: send its output once the socket is connected, and if the socket fails, call `connection(slot).closed()`. Panics when `slot` is not wanted or the pool is disposed. |
| `connection(slot: i32): PgConnection` | The connection in `slot`, its buffers the carrier's to fill and drain; the last one made after it fails. Panics when none was made. |
| `dispatch(): i32` | Hands the oldest waiting request to a ready connection with room (the one with the fewest in flight, or under `PgConfig.pack` the first), and answers its slot, `ticket` set to the request: build its group on `connection(slot)`, then `send()`. `PG_POOL_NONE` when nothing waits, a request is still being built, or no ready connection has room; then a connection may be wanted (`wanted()`): one more for every `maxInFlight` waiting requests that the connections already starting cannot take. A request handed out is the program's to end with `send()`: until then no other is handed out. |
| `dispose(): void` | Wipes the pool's password and every connection's; `connect` panics after it. |
| `inFlight(): i32` | The number of groups in flight on every connection, sent and not yet done: the `inFlight` a `PgBatchClock` reads. |
| `next(slot: i32): i32` | The next event from `slot`'s input, as `PgConnection.next()` answers it, `ticket` naming the request it is about (-1 for `PG_READY`, `PG_FAILED`, and a notice while no request is in flight). The `PG_DESCRIBED` of a registered statement is the pool's and is not answered. When the connection fails, `PG_LOST` comes for each request in flight on it, oldest first, then `PG_FAILED`: close its socket. A connection that fails before it is ready, while no other is, takes the oldest waiting request with it, so that a server that cannot be reached empties the queue rather than holds it. `PG_NEED_MORE` once `PG_FAILED` was answered, until `connect` builds the slot again. Panics as `connection(slot)` does. |
| `passwordWiped(): boolean` | Whether every byte of the pool's copy of the password is zero, as `PgConnection.passwordWiped()` reads its own. |
| `register(name: string, sql: string, paramTypes: i32[]): boolean` | Registers a statement for every connection to prepare before its first request. False when a connection has been made already, `name` or `sql` holds a NUL, or 256 are registered. |
| `request(): i32` | Queues a request and answers its ticket, or `PG_POOL_FULL` when `queueSize` are waiting. |
| `send(): boolean` | Ends the group of the request `dispatch()` handed out. False when there is none; when a bind is still open, so finish it and call again; and when no message of the group was written, so the request is dropped and gets no events (`PG_LOST` if its connection has failed). |
| `waiting(): i32` | The number of requests waiting for a connection. |
| `wanted(): i32` | A slot that needs a socket, or `PG_POOL_NONE`: connect it, then call `connect(slot, nonce)`. |

## PgTarget

Where a connection goes, from libpq's `host` and `port` or a
`postgres://` URL: `pgTarget` and `pgTargetUrl` make one, reading no
socket and no file. When `failure` is `PG_TARGET_OK`, a `unix` target is
`unixConnect(path)`, and any other is `host` and `port`, for
`netAddress` and `tcpConnect`.

A host starting with `/` is a socket directory, and one starting with `@`
a Linux abstract name, as in libpq: the socket is
`<host>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`. The host is always the directory, never the
socket file itself. Any other host is TCP.

```ts
class PgTarget
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgTarget()` |  |
| `failure: i32` | `PG_TARGET_OK`, or the `PG_TARGET_*` reason the input was refused. |
| `host: string` | The host as given (a URL's decoded, without an IPv6 address's brackets); for a socket, its directory or `@` name. |
| `path: string` | The socket's path, `<host>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`, when `unix`; otherwise "". |
| `port: i32` | The port: the TCP port, or the number in the socket's name. |
| `unix: boolean` | Whether the target is a Unix socket, at `path`. |

## PgText

Decoders for PostgreSQL's text format, in place; a bad input sets `failed`, which stays set.

```ts
class PgText
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgText()` |  |
| `failed: boolean` | Whether a decode since the last `reset()` was given something it could not read. |
| `bool(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): boolean` | A `bool` column: `t` or `f`; false and `failed` otherwise. |
| `int(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32): i64` | An `int2`, `int4` or `int8` column: an optional `-` and 1 to 19 digits; 0 and `failed` otherwise, and on overflow. |
| `reset(): void` | Clears `failed`. |
| `timestamp(b: u8[], start: i32, length: i32, out: u8[], at: i32): i32` | A `timestamptz` column, as the connection's `DateStyle=ISO` and `TimeZone=UTC` spell it (`2024-01-02 03:04:05.123456+00`), or a `timestamp` column (the same without `+00`), written to `out[at, at + 24)` as `2024-01-02T03:04:05.123Z`, the fraction cut to milliseconds. Answers 24, or -1 and `failed` for anything else: a year outside 0001–9999, BC, `infinity`, an offset other than `+00`. |

## Constants

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="-3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ARRAY_BAD: i32`

`PgArrayWalker.next()`: the text is not a one-dimensional array literal.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ARRAY_ELEMENT: i32`

`PgArrayWalker.next()`: an element, at `start` for `length` bytes.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ARRAY_END: i32`

`PgArrayWalker.next()`: no more elements.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ARRAY_NULL: i32`

`PgArrayWalker.next()`: a NULL element.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_DONE: i32`

`PgBatcher.next(run)`: the request `tag` has had all its rows, at least one.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_FAILED: i32`

`PgBatcher.next(run)`: the request `tag`'s execution failed, and its rows so far may be incomplete.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_INT: i32`

`PgBatchConfig.keyType`: the keys are `int8`, given to `PgBatcher.addInt`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_MISSING: i32`

`PgBatcher.next(run)`: no row answered the request `tag`'s key.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_NONE: i32`

`PgBatcher.next(run)`: no event until the next row, `end` or `fail`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_ROW: i32`

`PgBatcher.next(run)`: the connection's current row answers the request `tag`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_BATCH_TEXT: i32`

`PgBatchConfig.keyType`: the keys are `text`, given to `PgBatcher.addText`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_CLOCK_AVERAGE: i32`

`PgBatchClock.check`: the moving average of recent batches, times `factor`, is waiting.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_CLOCK_COUNT: i32`

`PgBatchClock.check`: `minCount` items are waiting, and the average asks no more.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_CLOCK_IDLE: i32`

`PgBatchClock.check`: nothing is in flight and little has arrived lately, so the item goes at once.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_CLOCK_TIMER: i32`

`PgBatchClock.check`: the oldest item has waited `maxWaitUs`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_CLOCK_WAIT: i32`

`PgBatchClock.check`: not yet; wait for an item or for `deadline()`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_COMPLETE: i32`

An execution has finished: `tagIs`, `tagRows`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="7" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_DESCRIBED: i32`

A prepared statement has been described: `columns`, `columnType(c)`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERROR: i32`

A statement in the current group failed: `lastError`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_AUTH_UNSUPPORTED: i32`

An authentication method this client refuses (cleartext, MD5, GSS, SSPI, a SASL mechanism other than SCRAM-SHA-256).

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="9" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_CLOSED: i32`

The program reported the end of the stream (`closed()`).

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_ENCODING: i32`

The server's `client_encoding` is not UTF8.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_FRAME: i32`

A message length below 4, or a message whose layout does not add up.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_NONE: i32`

`failure` while the connection is alive.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_SCRAM: i32`

A SCRAM exchange the server got wrong: a malformed message, a nonce that does not extend ours, an iteration count out of bounds.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="7" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_SERVER: i32`

The server sent a FATAL or PANIC error, or any error before the connection was ready: `lastError`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="6" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_SERVER_SIGNATURE: i32`

The server's SCRAM signature is not the one the password gives: it does not know the password.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="10" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_SETTING: i32`

The server's `DateStyle` is not ISO or its `TimeZone` is not UTC, the two the decoders read: at startup, or after a `SET`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_TOO_BIG: i32`

A message longer than `maxMessage`, or a row wider than `maxColumns`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ERR_UNEXPECTED: i32`

A message the protocol does not allow at this point.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_FAILED: i32`

Final: the connection is over, and `failure` says why.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_GROUP_DONE: i32`

A group has been answered: `groupFailed`, `txStatus`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="9" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_LOST: i32`

`PgPool.next(slot)`: the request `ticket` names will get no answer, because its connection failed first.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_NEED_MORE: i32`

`next()` needs more input before it can say anything.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="6" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_NOTICE: i32`

A notice: `lastNotice`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_POOL_FULL: i32`

`PgPool.request()`: the queue is full, and the request was not taken.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_POOL_NONE: i32`

`PgPool.dispatch()` and `PgPool.wanted()`: no slot.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_READY: i32`

The connection is authenticated and ready for queries; answered once.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ROW: i32`

A row: `columns` columns, each at `colStart(c)` for `colLength(c)` bytes.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_BAD_ESCAPE: i32`

`PgTarget.failure`: a `%` not followed by two hex digits, `%00`, or escapes that decode to bytes that are not UTF-8.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_BAD_HOST: i32`

`PgTarget.failure`: no host, more than one (a `,`), an unclosed `[` or text after its `]`, a raw `@` past the user information, or a NUL byte.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_BAD_PORT: i32`

`PgTarget.failure`: a port that is not 1 to 65535 in decimal digits.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_BAD_URL: i32`

`PgTarget.failure`: not a `postgres://` or `postgresql://` URL, or a query parameter with no `=`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_OK: i32`

`PgTarget.failure`: none; connect as `unix` says.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TARGET_TOO_LONG: i32`

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TURNS_FULL: i32`

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_TURNS_NONE: i32`

`PgBatchTurns`: no slot to wake.

</scalar-card>
